newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian rebels threaten fresh attacks in France.
newsitem.headline: Algerian rebels threaten fresh attacks in France.

text.p: Algeria's most ruthless Islamic rebel group has threatened to "destroy" France, confirming fears that the bombing of a Paris train which killed four commuters three weeks ago could signal a new wave of violence.

A senior official said on Tuesday that a letter to President Jacques Chirac purportedly from the Armed Islamic Group (GIA) vowed to "continue" attacks unless he intervened to free a GIA leader awaiting execution in Algeria.
The GIA said the French people were "among the worst enemies of Moslems" and told Chirac it would "destroy your country," the French daily Le Monde said, quoting from the letter.
The Interior Ministry confirmed that "a letter apparently coming from the GIA reached French authorities", adding that experts were working to verify it.
In an apparent reference to the December 3 rush-hour bombing of a commuter train at Paris' Port-Royal station, the GIA said, "We do what we say. The events of these last few days prove it."
Le Monde said the message was received overnight.
The Port-Royal bomb was a gas cannister filled with explosives and shrapnel, a technique used by the GIA in a wave of bombings which killed eight people in France last year.
"The government reiterates its condemnation of all forms of terrorism and its determination not to bow to blackmail, fear and violence," the Interior Ministry said in a statement.
The government's Anti-Terrorist Coordination Unit met on Tuesday and reiterated orders to government representatives across France to maintain the tightest possible security, the statement said.
It said 2,000 armed troops were guarding strategic buildings and helping police patrol train and metro stations and airports.

Police already face threats from Corsican separatists who have staged several bombings in mainland France in the past few weeks. They are suspected of planting a powerful bomb in a busy Marseille post office this week which failed to explode.
The GIA demanded that Chirac secure the release of GIA leader Abu-Adlan Abdelhaq Layada, extradited from Morocco to Algeria and sentenced to death in 1993, as well as other GIA members.
Roland Jacquard, who heads an international watchdog group monitoring terrorism, said the threats were troubling since the GIA knew Chirac had no way of securing Layada's release.
"It looks like another impossible demand, perhaps to make the French government appear responsible for what could happen," he said, adding it was not even clear if Layada was alive.
It was the fourth time the GIA had turned to France for help in obtaining Layada's release.
The group made the same demand at the height of last year's bombing wave in France, in a message which also urged Chirac to convert to Islam.
The demand was then repeated in March when GIA guerrillas kidnapped seven French monks in Algeria. The monks' throats were slit two months later.

The group first made the demand during the Christmas 1994 hijacking of a French airliner in Algiers. The four hijackers killed three passengers before being shot dead by French police after the plane landed in Marseille, southern France.

The GIA has accused France of backing Algeria's military authorities in a civil war that has claimed an estimated 60,000 lives since the government scrapped 1992 elections that Moslem fundamentalists were poised to win.

The group has claimed responsibility for killing dozens of foreigners in Algeria and the country's deadliest bomb attack, when a suicide bomber slammed a car into a police station in January 1995, killing 42 people.
